title: Africa
dates: Late in the second century to 312
datesNote: The map places the river's first tradition from 150, a placing year only. Eusebius lists bishops of Alexandria from Annianus, Mark's successor, in the eighth year of Nero, and gives Mark's founding as report. The era's end in 312 is the map's.
shortDescription: In this era the Africa river carries the church of Alexandria in Egypt. It holds the city's teachers, from Pantaenus and Clement to Origen, and its bishops through persecution and plague, down to Peter, beheaded in the Great Persecution.

parent.name: The First Churches
parent.basisInWords: declared: the tree sets it as growing from the first churches; its founding is obscure

directLine.childrenNote: No river leaves it in the origin records.

timeline.headline: What was said of the church's founding

lines.text: They say, Eusebius writes, that Mark was the first sent to Egypt, preached the Gospel he had written, and first set up churches in Alexandria.

lines.when: in the eighth year of Nero
lines.text: Annianus succeeds Mark the evangelist in charge of the church of Alexandria, Eusebius writes.

timeline.headline: Bishops and a school of teachers come into view

lines.when: in the first year of Commodus
lines.text: Julian becomes bishop of the churches of Alexandria.
Pantaenus, a man of great learning trained among the Stoics, has charge of the school of the faithful in Alexandria. Eusebius says such a school had stood there from ancient times.
Clement succeeds Pantaenus in charge of the instruction in Alexandria, and the boy Origen is one of his pupils.

timeline.headline: Origen, from a martyr's son to the head of the school

lines.text: A persecution reaches Alexandria. Leonides, father of Origen, is beheaded while his son is still young.
Origen takes charge of the school of instruction in the faith.

lines.when: in the tenth year of Alexander
lines.text: Origen moves from Alexandria to Caesarea, leaving the school to Heraclas.
lines.note: Eusebius says "the tenth year of the above-mentioned reign"; the reign last named is Alexander's.

timeline.headline: Dionysius leads the church through persecution and plague
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History, quoting Dionysius's letters for the persecution and the plague

lines.text: Dionysius, one of Origen's pupils, follows Heraclas in charge of the school.

lines.when: in the third year of Philip
lines.text: Heraclas dies, and Dionysius becomes bishop of the churches of Alexandria.
Dionysius writes that at Alexandria the persecution began a whole year before the emperor's decree.
After war and famine, a plague follows. Dionysius writes that most of the Christians nursed the sick without fear, and many died with them.

timeline.headline: The siege of the Pyrucheium, and Pamphilus at Caesarea

lines.text: In the siege of the Pyrucheium quarter of Alexandria, Anatolius gets the besieged out, those of the church first. Later he becomes a pastor at Laodicea in Syria.
At Caesarea in Palestine, in the time of Bishop Agapius, Eusebius comes to know Pamphilus.
Peter becomes bishop of Alexandria after Theonas had held the office for nineteen years.
Pamphilus, a presbyter of Caesarea, is put to death.
Peter, bishop of Alexandria, is seized without warning and beheaded, as if by order of Maximinus, and many bishops of Egypt die with him.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History IX.6.2, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 47990-47999; VIII.13.7, lines 44798-44802
lines.note: The census card of Peter gives 311.

peopleAndStories.note: Ordered by the census start years. In this era the Latin churches of Africa, at Carthage and Hippo, sit on the Latin West river, not this one.

howItBegan.reason: The church at Alexandria grew from the first churches; it is first seen clearly late in the second century. Its founding is obscure. The tradition that Mark founded it is reported by Eusebius as something people say.

sources.quote: they say that this Mark was the first that was sent to Egypt, and that he proclaimed the Gospel which he had written, and first established churches in Alexandria.

connections.note: Later links run out from Alexandria to the Latin West, the Greek East and the Non-Nicene traditions in era 2; each carries its own sources on its edge.

legacyAndToday.text: An episode of the church of Alexandria, which lives on today. The world built from this entry names the Coptic Orthodox Church as its main living heir.

uncertain: How it began. Its founding is obscure. Eusebius gives Mark's founding as something people say, and names Annianus as Mark's successor in the eighth year of Nero.

Whether there was one school. Eusebius, who says a school of sacred learning had stood there from ancient times and continued to his own day, calls the instruction a school and names the teacher in charge of it in each generation.
Where the river begins on the map. The year 150 only places the Alexandrian tradition; no old source gives it.
